title: Meteorology & Atmospheric Sciences
subtitle: Weather, climate & the physics of the atmosphere
methodology: METHODOLOGY · Every entry anchors to a landmark study, observation, dataset or theoretical text. The hint explains the idea in plain language; the note names the primary publication and flags replication status, revisions and known controversies. Studies and effects carry a replicability badge — 🟢 confirmed to high confidence · 🟡 nuanced, contested or partially revised · 🔴 failed or severely disputed. Map pins mark the field site, observatory or institution where the work was carried out.

categories.label: Theories & Models
categories.subtitle: The frameworks that organise how the atmosphere moves, heats and produces weather

entries.label: Frontal Theory (Bergen School)
entries.hint: Rather than treating weather as locally chaotic and essentially unpredictable, the Bergen School proposed that mid-latitude weather is organised around distinct boundaries, or 'fronts,' between air masses of different temperature and humidity — borrowing the wartime military term deliberately, since these boundaries were understood as genuine battle lines where colder and warmer air masses actively clash, and that a storm system's entire life cycle could be tracked and predicted by following how these fronts moved and interacted.
entries.note: Bjerknes, J. (1919). 'On the Structure of Moving Cyclones.' Monthly Weather Review, 47(2), 95–99, developed at the Bergen Geophysical Institute under his father Vilhelm Bjerknes. The frontal model, refined into the full Norwegian Cyclone Model (see th7) over the following years, transformed weather forecasting from a largely statistical, pattern-matching exercise into one grounded in an explicit physical model of how storms actually form and evolve.

entries.label: Adiabatic Lapse Rate Theory
entries.hint: As a parcel of air rises through the atmosphere, it expands into the lower surrounding pressure and cools — not because it loses heat to its surroundings, but purely because the work it does expanding uses up its own internal thermal energy — and this predictable cooling rate, roughly 10°C per kilometre for dry air but slower once condensation begins releasing latent heat, is the single physical mechanism underlying cloud formation, thunderstorm development, and why mountain tops are colder than valleys below.
entries.note: Espy, J.P. (1841). The Philosophy of Storms. Charles C. Little and James Brown, proposed that storms are driven by the latent heat released as rising, cooling, moist air condenses — an early, substantially correct convective theory of storm energy that was disputed for decades by rival theories favouring purely mechanical wave explanations for storm motion. The distinction between the dry adiabatic lapse rate and the slower moist adiabatic lapse rate remains fundamental to modern atmospheric stability analysis (see co1).

entries.label: Lorenz's Deterministic Chaos in Weather Prediction
entries.loc: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, Massachusetts
entries.hint: Running a simplified computer weather simulation a second time from what he thought were the exact same starting conditions, but had actually rounded to fewer decimal places for convenience, Lorenz found the model's forecast diverged completely from the original run within a simulated few weeks — revealing that weather is a genuinely chaotic system, in which even immeasurably tiny differences in starting conditions inevitably grow to swamp any forecast, placing a fundamental, unavoidable limit on how far in advance weather can ever be accurately predicted.
entries.note: Lorenz, E.N. (1963). 'Deterministic Nonperiodic Flow.' Journal of the Atmospheric Sciences, 20(2), 130–141, discovered the effect while running a simplified 12-equation weather model at MIT. The popularised 'butterfly effect' term and its broader mathematical framework as chaos theory are covered in depth in the systems-and-complexity folio; Lorenz's own specific finding was that this sensitivity imposes a practical predictability ceiling on weather forecasting of roughly two to three weeks, regardless of future advances in computing power or data collection.

entries.label: Bergeron-Findeisen Process
entries.hint: Inside a cold cloud containing both supercooled liquid water droplets and ice crystals, the ice crystals grow at the liquid droplets' direct expense, because ice requires a lower humidity to remain in equilibrium than liquid water does at the same sub-freezing temperature — meaning the air is simultaneously supersaturated with respect to ice while still undersaturated with respect to the liquid droplets, so water evaporates off the droplets and deposits directly onto the ice crystals, which grow rapidly enough to eventually fall as precipitation.
entries.note: Bergeron, T. (1933). 'On the Physics of Cloud and Precipitation.' Proceedings of the 5th Assembly of the International Union of Geodesy and Geophysics, 156–178, proposed the mechanism; Findeisen, W. (1938) provided further supporting observational and laboratory evidence. The process explains why most precipitation in the mid-latitudes, even warm summer rain, actually begins as ice crystals higher in the cloud that melt on the way down, rather than forming through liquid-droplet collision alone (see co3).

entries.label: General Circulation Theory
entries.hint: George Hadley proposed that the trade winds, and the broader pattern of global atmospheric circulation, arise from warm air rising at the equator and moving poleward at high altitude, cooling and sinking back down around 30 degrees latitude, then returning toward the equator near the surface — with the whole circulating loop deflected into the characteristic diagonal trade-wind pattern by Earth's rotation, the first physically grounded explanation for why global winds blow in consistent, predictable patterns rather than randomly.
entries.note: Hadley, G. (1735). 'Concerning the Cause of the General Trade-Winds.' Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, 39, 58–62. Hadley's original explanation for the wind deflection itself was subtly incorrect, correctly identified only much later once the Coriolis effect (see th6) was properly formalised; the basic circulating-cell structure he proposed, now called the Hadley cell, remains a foundational, largely accurate feature of the modern three-cell model of global atmospheric circulation.

entries.label: Coriolis Effect Theory
entries.hint: Any object moving across Earth's rotating surface appears, to an observer standing on that same rotating surface, to curve away from a straight-line path — deflecting to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere — not because any real sideways force is acting on it, but purely because the ground beneath it is itself rotating at a different speed depending on latitude, an apparent deflection that shapes the rotational direction of every hurricane, cyclone, and large-scale wind pattern on the planet.
entries.note: Coriolis, G.G. (1835). 'Sur les équations du mouvement relatif des systèmes de corps.' Journal de l'École Polytechnique, 15, 142–154, derived the effect mathematically in the context of rotating machinery, well before it was widely applied to atmospheric and oceanic circulation. The effect is exactly zero at the equator and strongest at the poles, which is why tropical cyclones (see ef4) essentially never form within about 5 degrees of the equator, regardless of how favourable the temperature and moisture conditions otherwise are.

entries.label: Norwegian Cyclone Model
entries.hint: Extending frontal theory (see th1) into a complete life-cycle model, the Bergen School proposed that mid-latitude storms develop in a predictable sequence of stages — a wave first forms along a stationary front between cold and warm air, the wave deepens into a full cyclone with connected warm and cold fronts, the faster-moving cold front eventually catches up to and 'occludes' the warm front, lifting the warm air entirely off the ground, and the storm finally dissipates as its temperature contrast is exhausted — a stage-by-stage model still taught to every meteorology student today.
entries.note: Bjerknes, J. & Solberg, H. (1922). 'Life Cycle of Cyclones and the Polar Front Theory of Atmospheric Circulation.' Geofysiske Publikasjoner, 3(1), 1–18. The model was developed using an unusually dense observational network of volunteer weather stations established across Norway specifically to track storms in fine spatial detail, a methodological innovation nearly as significant to the theory's success as the physical insight itself.

entries.label: CAPE / Convective Instability Theory
entries.loc: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, Massachusetts
entries.hint: Whether the atmosphere on a given day will support explosive thunderstorm development depends on how much excess heat energy a rising parcel of air would have compared to its surrounding environment at each altitude — if a lifted parcel stays warmer, and therefore less dense, than the air around it all the way up, it keeps accelerating upward, and the total accumulated energy available for that acceleration, integrated through the whole atmospheric column, quantifies exactly how violent a thunderstorm the atmosphere is primed to produce.
entries.note: Rossby, C.-G. (1932). 'Thermodynamics Applied to Air Mass Analysis.' MIT Professional Notes, No. 1, formalised parcel theory and atmospheric instability analysis. The modern quantitative metric, Convective Available Potential Energy (CAPE), built directly on this parcel-theory foundation and is now calculated automatically from every weather balloon sounding worldwide, providing forecasters a single number summarising a region's thunderstorm potential for the day.

entries.label: Baroclinic Instability Theory
entries.hint: Where a strong horizontal temperature gradient exists in the atmosphere — most prominently along the boundary between cold polar air and warm subtropical air — the atmosphere becomes inherently unstable in a specific way that spontaneously generates travelling waves and eventually full storm systems, converting the stored potential energy of the temperature contrast itself into the kinetic energy of circulating winds, explaining why mid-latitude storms reliably form along the jet stream rather than at random locations.
entries.note: Charney, J.G. (1947). 'The Dynamics of Long Waves in a Baroclinic Westerly Current.' Journal of Meteorology, 4(5), 135–162, provided the first mathematically rigorous theory of how these waves grow; Eady, E.T. (1949) independently developed a related, more simplified model two years later. Baroclinic instability theory directly explains the jet stream's wavy, meandering path and remains foundational to modern numerical weather prediction models (see me3, me4) of mid-latitude storm development.

entries.label: Rayleigh Scattering (Atmospheric Optics)
entries.hint: Sunlight passing through the atmosphere is scattered by air molecules far more strongly at shorter wavelengths than longer ones, scattering blue light many times more effectively than red — explaining both why the daytime sky appears blue in every direction, since scattered blue light reaches the eye from all across the sky, and why sunsets appear red, since the much longer path sunlight travels through the atmosphere at a low sun angle scatters away nearly all the blue light before it reaches an observer, leaving mostly the less-scattered red and orange wavelengths.
entries.note: Strutt, J.W. (Lord Rayleigh) (1871). 'On the Light from the Sky, its Polarization and Colour.' Philosophical Magazine, 41(271), 107–120, derived the wavelength-dependent scattering relationship mathematically. The same principle explains why the sky on Mars, with its thin, dust-laden atmosphere, appears a dusty butterscotch colour rather than blue during the day, while its sunsets can appear distinctly blue — essentially the reverse pattern from Earth's.

categories.label: Landmark Studies
categories.subtitle: The defining experiments — and exactly what they found

entries.label: FitzRoy's Storm Warning Service
entries.hint: Robert FitzRoy, the former captain of HMS Beagle turned first head of the newly created UK Meteorological Department, established the world's first operational storm-warning system, using telegraph reports from coastal stations to track approaching weather and issue advance warnings to ships and ports — the first systematic, government-run attempt to actually forecast the weather rather than merely record it after the fact.
entries.note: FitzRoy, R. established the Met Office storm warning system in 1861, coining the term 'weather forecast' itself, and began publishing daily forecasts in The Times newspaper the same year. FitzRoy's forecasts drew sustained public ridicule from scientific peers sceptical that weather could be meaningfully predicted at all, and the psychological strain of this criticism, combined with prior struggles, contributed to his suicide in 1865; forecasting was briefly suspended afterward before resuming permanently.

entries.label: Richardson's Numerical Weather Prediction Attempt
entries.hint: Attempting to forecast the weather purely by solving the physical equations governing atmospheric motion by hand, using six weeks of tedious arithmetic to calculate just a single six-hour forecast for one region, Richardson produced a wildly, absurdly inaccurate result — predicting an implausible surge in atmospheric pressure that never remotely happened — but his approach of treating weather prediction as a solvable system of physical equations, rather than pattern-matching against historical analogues, correctly anticipated the entire future of numerical weather forecasting.
entries.note: Richardson, L.F. (1922). Weather Prediction by Numerical Process. Cambridge University Press. The failure was later diagnosed as resulting from unfiltered high-frequency noise in his initial atmospheric pressure data, a problem only properly solved decades later once computers made it practical to apply mathematical filtering techniques Richardson himself lacked the computational power to implement. Richardson's famous, only half-joking vision of a 'forecast factory' — 64,000 human computers working in a giant hall to calculate weather forecasts faster than the weather itself unfolds — anticipated the basic parallel-computing structure of every modern weather model.

entries.label: ENIAC First Computer Weather Forecast
entries.hint: A team led by meteorologist Jule Charney used the world's first general-purpose electronic computer to calculate a 24-hour weather forecast — the calculation itself took about 24 hours to run, meaning the computer forecast the weather no faster than the weather actually happened, but it worked, successfully reproducing key features of an already-observed historical storm and proving numerical weather prediction (see st2) was genuinely computationally feasible, not merely theoretically sound.
entries.note: Charney, J.G., Fjørtoft, R. & von Neumann, J. (1950). 'Numerical Integration of the Barotropic Vorticity Equation.' Tellus, 2(4), 237–254, ran on the ENIAC computer at Aberdeen Proving Ground in Maryland. The team deliberately used a highly simplified single-layer atmospheric model to keep the calculation computationally tractable; the experiment's practical success directly launched the field of operational numerical weather prediction, which within a decade became standard practice at national weather services worldwide.

entries.label: The Tri-State Tornado
entries.hint: A single tornado tracked continuously along the ground for roughly 350 kilometres across Missouri, Illinois, and Indiana — by far the longest confirmed continuous tornado path on record — killing 695 people, still the deadliest single tornado in United States history, and its extraordinary scale and destructiveness became a foundational case study driving the eventual development of organised tornado warning systems decades later.
entries.note: The tornado struck on 18 March 1925; contemporary analysis was limited by the era's sparse observation network and lack of any real-time warning capability, since the US Weather Bureau at the time actively discouraged the word 'tornado' in forecasts for fear of causing panic. Modern reanalysis (Johns, R.H. et al. 2013, and other studies) has debated whether the damage path represents one continuous tornado or a rapid succession of several distinct tornadoes from the same parent storm, a question the era's evidence cannot fully settle either way.

entries.label: The Galveston Hurricane
entries.hint: A powerful hurricane struck Galveston, Texas — then a major port city built on a low, flat barrier island with no seawall — with almost no advance public warning, killing an estimated 6,000 to 12,000 people in a single night, still the deadliest natural disaster in United States history by a wide margin, and the catastrophe directly drove the construction of a massive protective seawall and a fundamental overhaul of US hurricane forecasting and warning procedures in the decades that followed.
entries.note: The hurricane struck on 8 September 1900; the US Weather Bureau's chief forecaster in Galveston, Isaac Cline, had earlier publicly argued a serious hurricane strike on the city was virtually impossible. The disaster's staggering death toll directly catalysed the construction of the 3-metre Galveston Seawall, completed in 1904, and prompted the Weather Bureau to substantially improve its hurricane tracking and warning communication, though a fully modern hurricane warning system would still take decades longer to develop.

entries.label: Fujita's Downburst Discovery
entries.hint: Investigating a mysterious pattern of wind damage from a 1975 airliner crash — trees and structures blown outward in a distinctive radiating starburst pattern rather than the rotational pattern a tornado leaves — Fujita identified an entirely new, previously unrecognised weather phenomenon: a sudden, powerful, localised downward burst of wind plunging out of a thunderstorm and slamming into the ground, spreading outward in every direction, a hazard aviation had been unknowingly flying into for years.
entries.note: Fujita, T.T. (1976). 'Spearhead Echo and Downburst Near the Approach End of a John F. Kennedy Airport Runway, New York City.' Satellite and Mesometeorology Research Project, University of Chicago, Research Paper No. 137. Fujita's downburst concept was initially met with considerable scepticism from the meteorological community until confirmed by dedicated field research projects (NIMROD, 1978; JAWS, 1982); the discovery directly led to onboard and ground-based wind-shear detection systems now standard at major airports worldwide, substantially reducing microburst-related aviation accidents.

entries.label: Discovery of the Jet Stream
entries.hint: Systematically tracking weather balloons launched from Japan, Ōishi documented a narrow, remarkably fast river of high-altitude wind, regularly exceeding 200 kilometres per hour, meandering across the upper atmosphere — a discovery published only in Esperanto and consequently overlooked for years outside Japan, until Allied bomber crews flying at high altitude over Japan during the Second World War rediscovered the same powerful winds firsthand, sometimes finding their aircraft blown backward relative to the ground despite flying at full forward airspeed.
entries.note: Ōishi, W. (1926 onward, published 1941 in Esperanto specifically to reach an international audience without language barriers). 'Pilot Balloon Observations at the Base of the JOO Sounding.' The jet stream's global significance was not widely appreciated until American bomber pilots targeting Japan in 1944 reported unexpectedly severe headwinds and tailwinds that dramatically affected bombing accuracy and fuel consumption, and postwar meteorologists connected the observations directly back to Ōishi's earlier, overlooked balloon data.

entries.label: Walker's Discovery of the Southern Oscillation
entries.hint: Tasked with finding a way to predict the Indian monsoon's notoriously variable strength after a series of devastating famine-causing failures, Walker instead discovered something different: a seesawing pattern of atmospheric pressure between the eastern and western tropical Pacific Ocean, where pressure rising on one side reliably coincided with pressure falling on the other — a large-scale atmospheric pattern he could not fully explain at the time, but that later research connected directly to the ocean-temperature cycle known as El Niño.
entries.note: Walker, G.T. (1923). 'Correlation in Seasonal Variations of Weather, VIII: A Preliminary Study of World Weather.' Memoirs of the India Meteorological Department, 24, 75–131. Walker's statistical correlation was widely dismissed as a curious numerical coincidence for decades, lacking any known physical mechanism, until Jacob Bjerknes (1969, Monthly Weather Review) connected it directly to ocean-atmosphere coupling and the El Niño sea-surface temperature cycle, formally establishing what is now called the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO).

entries.label: Union City Doppler Radar Tornado Observation
entries.hint: Experimental Doppler radar, capable of directly measuring wind velocity rather than just precipitation intensity, tracked a tornado-producing thunderstorm near Union City, Oklahoma, from its earliest formative rotation through the tornado's full life cycle and eventual dissipation — the first time researchers had observed a tornadic storm's internal wind structure directly and continuously, revealing the signature rotating wind pattern, later called a 'mesocyclone,' that precedes tornado formation by many minutes.
entries.note: Researchers at the National Severe Storms Laboratory in Norman, Oklahoma, documented the 24 May 1973 Union City tornado using experimental Doppler radar (Brown, R.A., Lemon, L.R. & Burgess, D.W. 1978, Monthly Weather Review). The clear, reliable mesocyclone signature identified in this and subsequent storms directly justified the decades-long, multi-billion-dollar national investment in deploying the operational Doppler radar network (see me1) that now underlies every US tornado warning issued today.

entries.label: TIROS-1 First Weather Satellite
entries.hint: The first satellite purpose-built to observe Earth's weather from orbit transmitted the first-ever televised images of cloud cover from space, immediately proving that continuous, whole-planet observation of storm systems — including remote ocean regions with no ships or ground stations to report from at all — was not just possible but immediately, dramatically useful, spotting a previously unknown tropical storm in its very first days of operation.
entries.note: TIROS-1 (Television Infrared Observation Satellite) launched on 1 April 1960 and operated for just 78 days before a hardware failure ended its mission, but transmitted over 19,000 images of cloud cover during that short window. The satellite's demonstrated ability to track storm systems over data-sparse ocean regions, where hurricanes had previously often gone undetected until making landfall, directly launched the now-essential field of satellite meteorology that underlies virtually all modern tropical cyclone tracking (see ap3).

entries.label: Halley's Trade Wind Chart
entries.hint: Compiling data from ships' logbooks recording wind direction across the tropical Atlantic and Indian Oceans, Halley produced the first systematic map of the trade winds and monsoon patterns, demonstrating that these winds blow in remarkably consistent, predictable directions across enormous swaths of open ocean — a purely empirical, descriptive achievement published nearly fifty years before Hadley (see th5) would attempt to actually explain why the winds behaved this way.
entries.note: Halley, E. (1686). 'An Historical Account of the Trade Winds, and Monsoons, Observable in the Seas Between and Near the Tropics.' Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, 16, 153–168. Halley correctly identified solar heating of the equatorial atmosphere as the trade winds' underlying energy source but did not attempt to explain the winds' characteristic diagonal, rather than straight north-south, direction, a gap Hadley's later theoretical framework would address.

entries.label: The 1953 North Sea Flood
entries.hint: An unusually intense storm combined with an exceptionally high spring tide to push a devastating storm surge onto the low-lying coastlines of the Netherlands, England, and Belgium, breaching sea defences in hundreds of places and killing over 2,500 people — the disaster directly exposed how a specific, dangerous combination of meteorological and astronomical factors could compound into a catastrophe far worse than either factor alone, and drove the Netherlands to build the Delta Works, one of history's largest storm-surge protection engineering projects.
entries.note: The storm struck on the night of 31 January – 1 February 1953. The disaster directly catalysed the establishment of dedicated storm surge forecasting services across the North Sea region, combining meteorological wind and pressure forecasts with tidal and coastal bathymetry data to predict flood risk — a forecasting discipline distinct from ordinary weather prediction that remains essential to modern coastal flood warning systems in low-lying regions worldwide.

entries.label: Vilhelm Bjerknes's Weather-as-Physics-Problem Manifesto
entries.hint: Bjerknes argued that if the atmosphere's exact current state could be measured precisely enough, and the physical laws governing fluid motion and thermodynamics were known precisely enough, then the future weather should in principle be exactly calculable, the same way an astronomer calculates a planet's future position — reframing weather forecasting from an art of pattern recognition and intuition into, at least in principle, a solvable problem in physics and mathematics.
entries.note: Bjerknes, V. (1904). 'Das Problem der Wettervorhersage, betrachtet vom Standpunkte der Mechanik und der Physik.' Meteorologische Zeitschrift, 21, 1–7. Bjerknes correctly identified the two practical obstacles blocking his vision — insufficiently precise real-time atmospheric observations, and the sheer volume of calculation required — decades before either problem could actually be solved; his son Jacob Bjerknes (see th1, th7) and the wider Bergen School he founded turned the elder Bjerknes's theoretical manifesto into practical, working forecasting methods.

categories.label: Effects & Phenomena
categories.subtitle: Named, replicable patterns in atmospheric and weather behaviour

entries.label: Foehn Wind Effect
entries.hint: As moist air is forced up and over a mountain range, it cools at the slower moist adiabatic rate while releasing its moisture as precipitation on the windward slope, but once it crests the peak and descends the leeward side, the now much drier air warms back up at the faster dry adiabatic rate — arriving at the base of the mountain's far side dramatically warmer and drier than it started, a warm, gusty downslope wind that can raise temperatures by 10-20°C within an hour and rapidly melt snow.
entries.note: Hann, J. von (1866). 'Zur Frage über den Ursprung des Föhn.' Zeitschrift der Österreichischen Gesellschaft für Meteorologie, 1, 257–263, provided the first physically correct thermodynamic explanation, building on the differing dry and moist adiabatic lapse rates (see th2). The same phenomenon occurs worldwide under different regional names — the chinook in the Rocky Mountains, the zonda in Argentina, the Santa Ana in Southern California — and can trigger rapid, dangerous increases in wildfire risk due to the sudden drop in humidity and rise in wind speed.

entries.label: Temperature Inversion
entries.hint: Normally, air temperature decreases steadily with altitude, letting warm air near the ground rise freely and disperse; but under certain conditions — often a clear, calm night allowing the ground to radiate away its heat rapidly — a layer of unusually warm air can form above a colder layer near the surface, inverting the normal pattern and creating an invisible lid that traps cold air, fog, smoke, and pollution close to the ground, unable to rise and disperse until the inversion eventually breaks down.
entries.note: The 1930 Meuse Valley fog disaster in Belgium, in which an unusually persistent multi-day temperature inversion trapped industrial pollution in a narrow valley and killed at least 60 people, was among the first air-pollution disasters scientifically documented as directly attributable to inversion-trapped stagnant air (Firket, J. 1931, Bulletin de l'Académie Royale de Médecine de Belgique). Similar inversion-trapped pollution events, including the 1952 London smog, follow the same basic atmospheric mechanism.

entries.label: Lake Effect Snow
entries.hint: When a mass of cold, dry air moves across a relatively warm, unfrozen lake, it picks up substantial moisture and heat from the water surface below, becoming increasingly unstable as it travels, and dumps that moisture as intense, narrow bands of heavy snow once the destabilised air reaches the far shore and is forced to rise — producing localised snowfall totals that can be dramatically higher just a few kilometres inland from the lake than areas only slightly further away outside the narrow band's path.
entries.note: Peace, R.L. & Sykes, R.B. (1966). 'Mesoscale Study of a Lake Effect Snow Storm.' Monthly Weather Review, 94(8), 495–507, documented the narrow-band structure using radar data from the Great Lakes region. The effect requires the temperature difference between the lake surface and the air passing over it to exceed a threshold of roughly 13°C, which is why lake-effect snow is heaviest in early winter before the lake itself eventually freezes over and shuts off its own moisture and heat source.

entries.label: Tropical Cyclone Formation Threshold
entries.hint: A tropical cyclone can only form and intensify where several specific conditions coincide simultaneously: ocean surface water warmer than about 26.5°C to at least 50 metres depth, enough Coriolis deflection (see th6) to initiate rotation, meaning at least a few degrees away from the equator, low wind shear so the storm's vertical structure isn't torn apart as it grows, and sufficiently moist mid-level air — when even one of these conditions is absent, no amount of the others can compensate, which is why hurricanes reliably form only in specific ocean basins during specific seasons.
entries.note: Palmén, E. (1948). 'On the Formation and Structure of Tropical Hurricanes.' Geophysica, 3, 26–38, identified the 26.5°C sea-surface temperature threshold now named after him. All these conditions being individually necessary but not sufficient means meteorologists can identify large regions and seasons of elevated hurricane risk well in advance, even though which specific weak disturbance among many will actually organise into a named storm remains considerably harder to predict.

entries.label: Microburst Wind Shear
entries.hint: A microburst is a highly localised, intensely concentrated downdraft, often less than 4 kilometres across, that slams into the ground and spreads outward at speeds sometimes exceeding 150 kilometres per hour — extremely dangerous specifically to aircraft during takeoff or landing, since a plane flying through one first experiences a sudden, deceptive headwind that increases lift, immediately followed by an equally sudden tailwind and downdraft that can cause a catastrophic, unrecoverable loss of altitude within seconds.
entries.note: The 1982 Joint Airport Weather Studies (JAWS) project near Denver, Colorado, used dedicated Doppler radar networks to systematically document dozens of microbursts, confirming and quantifying Fujita's original hypothesis (see st6). Several major commercial airline crashes through the 1970s and 1980s were subsequently reattributed to microburst wind shear, directly driving the installation of dedicated wind-shear detection radar at major airports worldwide.

entries.label: Halo & Sundog Optical Phenomena
entries.hint: High, thin cirrus clouds are made of tiny, hexagonal ice crystals rather than liquid water droplets, and when sunlight or moonlight passes through these crystals it refracts at very specific, predictable angles determined by the hexagonal crystal geometry — producing a ring of light circling the sun or moon at almost exactly 22 degrees radius, and sometimes two especially bright spots, called sundogs, positioned exactly at that same 22-degree distance to either side of the sun itself.
entries.note: Descartes, R. (1637). Les Météores, an appendix to Discours de la méthode, provided an early mathematical treatment of halo geometry using ray-tracing through simplified ice-crystal shapes. The specific 22-degree radius is a direct, fixed geometric consequence of the hexagonal ice crystal's refractive index and prism angle, essentially identical to the mechanism producing a rainbow from spherical raindrops but with a different, more consistent characteristic angle since ice crystals have a far more regular geometric shape than water droplets.

entries.label: The Green Flash
entries.hint: In the last second or two before the sun fully disappears below a distant, unobstructed horizon, on a very clear day, a brief flash of green light can sometimes be seen right at the sun's upper edge — caused by the atmosphere acting like a weak prism, bending the sun's different colours by very slightly different amounts, so that by the moment the red and orange light has already dropped below the horizon, only the still-visible green (and, more rarely, blue) light remains briefly detectable at the sun's rim.
entries.note: O'Connell, D.J.K. (1958). The Green Flash and Other Low Sun Phenomena. Vatican Observatory Publications, provided the first rigorous photographic and spectroscopic study of the phenomenon, confirming it as a genuine atmospheric-refraction effect rather than a purely optical illusion or eye artefact, as some contemporaries had suspected. The flash requires an extremely clear, distant, unobstructed horizon, most commonly seen over open ocean, and typically lasts only one to two seconds, making it notoriously easy to miss.

entries.label: Sea Breeze / Land Breeze Cycle
entries.hint: Land heats up and cools down far faster than water does, so during a sunny day coastal land becomes warmer than the adjacent sea, and the warm air rising over land draws in cooler air from over the water to replace it — a daytime sea breeze blowing from water to land — while at night the pattern reverses entirely, as the now-relatively-warmer sea draws in cooler air flowing outward from the faster-cooling land in a nighttime land breeze, a reliable daily cycle familiar to anyone who has spent a full day at a beach.
entries.note: Simpson, J.E. (1994). Sea Breeze and Local Winds. Cambridge University Press, remains the definitive modern scientific synthesis of the phenomenon's dynamics, building on much earlier qualitative descriptions including Edmond Halley's own 1686 trade-wind paper (see st11). Sea breezes can penetrate over 100 kilometres inland in some regions and are strong enough to trigger their own localised thunderstorm development where the advancing breeze front lifts humid air, a mechanism forecasters in coastal regions, including Florida, watch for daily.

entries.label: Sudden Stratospheric Warming
entries.hint: Occasionally, in the middle of winter, the normally frigid polar stratosphere can warm dramatically and rapidly — by as much as 30-50°C within just a few days — as a wave disturbance from the lower atmosphere disrupts and sometimes completely reverses the usual westerly polar vortex winds circling the pole, an event that, despite happening tens of kilometres above the ground, can subsequently disrupt the jet stream and drive severe cold-air outbreaks at the surface far to the south for weeks afterward.
entries.note: Scherhag, R. (1952). 'Die explosionsartigen Stratosphärenerwärmungen des Spätwinters 1951/52.' Berichte des Deutschen Wetterdienstes in der US-Zone, 6(38), 51–63, first documented the phenomenon over Berlin. The connection between a stratospheric warming event and subsequent severe surface cold snaps typically takes two to six weeks to fully manifest, giving forecasters a genuine, if imperfect, extended early-warning signal for major cold-air outbreaks well beyond the normal weather forecasting horizon (see db8).

categories.label: Key Concepts
categories.subtitle: The building blocks and vocabulary every student must command

entries.label: Atmospheric Stability
entries.hint: Comparing how fast a lifted air parcel cools (see th2) against how fast the surrounding environmental air actually changes temperature with height reveals whether the atmosphere on a given day is stable, actively resisting vertical air movement and keeping the sky calm and layered, unstable, readily allowing air to keep rising and building towering storm clouds, or conditionally unstable, stable for dry air but unstable once condensation begins releasing extra latent heat — a single comparison that determines almost everything about a day's weather character.
entries.note: Petterssen, S. (1940). Weather Analysis and Forecasting. McGraw-Hill, systematised the stable/unstable/conditionally unstable classification framework still taught in every introductory meteorology course. Forecasters routinely compare the environmental temperature profile measured by a weather balloon sounding (see me2) against the dry and moist adiabatic lapse rates plotted on the same chart to directly read off a day's stability classification and thunderstorm potential.

entries.label: Air Mass Classification
entries.hint: A large body of air sitting for days or weeks over a relatively uniform surface region — a frozen arctic ice sheet, a warm tropical ocean, a dry continental desert — gradually takes on that source region's characteristic temperature and humidity throughout its entire depth, and once it eventually moves away from its source region, it carries those acquired characteristics with it, so classifying an air mass by where it originated predicts much of what kind of weather it will bring wherever it travels next.
entries.note: Bergeron, T. (1928). 'Über die dreidimensional verknüpfende Wetteranalyse.' Geofysiske Publikasjoner, 5(6), developed the standard letter-coded air mass classification system (for example 'cP' for continental polar, 'mT' for maritime tropical) still used in weather analysis today. The boundary where two different air masses meet is precisely what defines a weather front (see th1), making air mass classification and frontal theory two directly complementary halves of the same analytical framework.

entries.label: Cloud Classification
entries.hint: Howard classified clouds into a small number of basic shape categories, named in Latin — cirrus for wispy, thread-like high clouds, cumulus for puffy, heaped clouds, stratus for flat, layered sheets, and nimbus for a rain-bearing cloud — that could be combined to describe the enormous variety of actual clouds observed, giving meteorologists worldwide a shared, precise, universally understood vocabulary in place of the vague, purely descriptive folk terms used previously.
entries.note: Howard, L. (1803). 'On the Modification of Clouds.' Philosophical Magazine, 16, 97–107, established the Latin naming system still used today, with only modest later refinement. The poet Johann Wolfgang von Goethe was reportedly so impressed by Howard's classification that he wrote a set of poems in tribute to it; Howard's system also directly organises cloud height into three families — high, middle, and low — that correspond closely to the different temperature and moisture regimes at each altitude (see th4).

entries.label: The Enhanced Fujita Scale
entries.hint: Since a tornado's actual wind speed can almost never be measured directly at the moment of peak intensity, tornado strength is instead estimated indirectly, after the fact, by carefully surveying the specific type and severity of structural damage left behind — comparing how badly different, standardised types of buildings and objects were damaged against a detailed reference guide that translates observed damage severity into an estimated wind speed range.
entries.note: McDonald, J.R. & Mehta, K.C. (2006). 'A Recommendation for an Enhanced Fujita Scale.' Texas Tech University, Wind Science and Engineering Center, refined Ted Fujita's original 1971 damage scale (see fg6) using 28 distinct damage indicators, from mobile homes to well-built brick structures, each with its own detailed severity table. The Enhanced Fujita Scale was formally adopted by the US National Weather Service in 2007 and provides substantially more consistent, defensible ratings than the original scale's broader, more subjective damage categories.

entries.label: The Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale
entries.hint: Hurricanes are sorted into five categories purely by their maximum sustained wind speed, from a minimal Category 1 to a catastrophic Category 5, giving the public and emergency planners an immediately recognisable, single-number severity rating — though the scale deliberately says nothing directly about a specific storm's rainfall, storm surge height, or physical size, all factors that can make a lower-category storm considerably more dangerous and destructive than the wind-speed number alone might suggest.
entries.note: Saffir, H. (1971), a structural engineer, developed the original wind-speed-based category scale for a United Nations report on housing damage; Simpson, R.H., then director of the National Hurricane Center, added storm-surge and general impact descriptions. Hurricane Harvey (2017), a Category 4 storm at landfall, caused catastrophic flooding damage from rainfall alone that vastly exceeded many higher-category storms, a widely cited example of the scale's inherent limitation in only capturing wind speed.

entries.label: Dew Point & Relative Humidity
entries.hint: Relative humidity describes how close the air currently is to being fully saturated with water vapour, as a percentage of the maximum it could hold at that specific temperature — but because warmer air can hold far more moisture than cold air, the same relative humidity percentage represents very different actual moisture amounts at different temperatures, which is why meteorologists also track dew point, the specific temperature air would need to cool to in order to become fully saturated, a far more direct and temperature-independent measure of how much moisture is actually present.
entries.note: Daniell, J.F. (1820). 'On a New Hygrometer, which Measures the Dew Point.' Quarterly Journal of Science, Literature and the Arts, 8, 298–305, provided a practical instrument for direct dew-point measurement. Dew point is widely considered a more reliable indicator of how muggy or humid a day will actually feel than relative humidity alone, since a dew point above about 20°C generally feels noticeably uncomfortable regardless of the accompanying temperature or relative-humidity percentage reading.

entries.label: Synoptic Scale vs. Mesoscale
entries.hint: Atmospheric phenomena naturally sort into a hierarchy of characteristic sizes and lifespans, and different observation and forecasting tools are needed at each scale — synoptic-scale systems like a mid-latitude cyclone span a thousand kilometres and last several days, readily visible on a standard weather map, while mesoscale phenomena like a single thunderstorm or a sea breeze front span just a few to a few hundred kilometres and last only hours, requiring denser, more specialised local monitoring to detect and forecast at all.
entries.note: Orlanski, I. (1975). 'A Rational Subdivision of Scales for Atmospheric Processes.' Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society, 56(5), 527–530, formalised the now-standard micro-, meso-, synoptic-, and planetary-scale classification framework. The distinction matters practically because a numerical weather model's grid resolution (see me3, me4) must be fine enough to actually capture a given phenomenon's characteristic scale — a coarse global model can miss a dangerous, fast-developing local thunderstorm entirely even while accurately forecasting the broader synoptic-scale pattern around it.

entries.label: Albedo
entries.hint: Albedo measures what fraction of incoming sunlight a surface reflects straight back to space rather than absorbing as heat, expressed as a simple number between 0 (a perfectly absorbing black surface) and 1 (a perfectly reflecting white surface) — fresh snow reflects 80-90% of sunlight, giving it a very high albedo, while dark ocean water absorbs the great majority of the sunlight hitting it, giving it a very low albedo, a simple physical property that plays an outsized role in regional and global temperature patterns.
entries.note: Lambert, J.H. (1760). Photometria. Augsburg, established the foundational mathematics of surface reflectance later applied specifically to atmospheric and climate science. Clouds themselves have a substantial average albedo of roughly 0.3 to 0.6 depending on thickness and type, meaning cloud cover plays a major, still not perfectly quantified role in Earth's overall energy balance — an active area of ongoing atmospheric research given how difficult clouds remain to represent accurately in large-scale weather and climate models.
